messages.subject: Volume Forms and Radon-Nikodym
parts:
I was reading through "Identifying the Optimal Integration Time in
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo" and had to go back to "The Geometric Foundations of
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo" to follow (some of) the notation.

I am sure I will have plenty more questions but can someone confirm
that in 1.1 of the former and 3.1 of the latter that the right hand
side is the Radon-Nikodym derivative? Here’s the equation in LaTeX but
I doubt googlegroups will render it :(

$$
H = -\log\frac{d(\pi^*\bar{\omega} \wedge \zeta)}{d\Omega}
$$

I think it has to be because $\Omega$ is volume form and the
differential of such a form is 0 so using $d$ to denote differential
makes no sense (even if the ratio of k-forms made any sense).

But in that case, how is the Radon-Nikodym derivative being
calculated? Presumably in some co-ordinate system (the canonical
co-ordinate system?), we can associate (real-valued) functions on the
cotangent bundle, now interpreted as a measure space, with the two
volume forms? I assume that this concept is well-defined with respect
to changes in co-ordinates?

Great papers BTW

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Volume Forms and Radon-Nikodym
parts:
On Sunday, 22 January 2017 17:57:41 UTC, idontgetoutmuch wrote:
Great! - My next question is what does the LaTeX symbol \lrcorner denote? Also in Lemma 10 of "The Geometric Foundations of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo" I am not sure what to make of the denominator? I assume it is a "smooth" measure which is thus an n-form and therefore applying it to n vector fields (the frame) produce a real number?

Answering my own question, I think this symbol is being used to denote the interior product so presumably Cartan's formula ($\mathcal{L}_X\omega = i_Xd\omega + d(i_X \omega)$) in this notation would read $\mathcal{L}_X\omega = X \lrcorner d\omega + d(X \lrcorner \omega)$.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Volume Forms and Radon-Nikodym
parts: > Great! - My next question is what does the LaTeX symbol \lrcorner denote?
As noted in another of your emails, it denotes the interior product.

> Also in Lemma 10 of "The Geometric Foundations of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo" I am not sure what to make of the denominator? I assume it is a "smooth" measure which is thus an n-form and therefore applying it to n vector fields (the frame) produce a real number?

Yes, mu_{Q} is an n-form that contracts against X horizontal vector
fields to yield a scalar function. Perhaps more intuitively, mu_{Q}
restricts to a smooth measure on the base space which defines
the geometric equivalent of marginalization.
